summary: Ezekiel sees a man place a mark on the foreheads of those who lament what is happening in Jerusalem. Job calls attention to his own mark when he asks for a hearing. In Daniel, the Aramaic verb describes the king’s astonishment at seeing four men walking in the furnace.

senses.definition: A sign placed on a person so that the bearer can be recognised.

evidence.note: The mark is put on the forehead. Those who bear it are to be spared.

senses.definition: A mark of attestation. Job presents his case as though he has set his mark to a written declaration.

evidence.note: Job asks for a hearing and a written statement from his accuser.

senses.definition: Place a visible sign on a person. The verb takes the related noun תָּו as its object.

evidence.note: The writer is told to go through Jerusalem marking those who sigh and groan.

senses.definition: Describe the effect of Israel’s repeated testing of God. The parallel and the preceding verse suggest the pain of rebellion.

evidence.note: The first half of the line speaks of testing God. Verse 40 has already described grieving him.

words.summary: This sense rests on a single verse. How it relates to marking is uncertain.

senses.definition: One reading gives the distant limit reached by the blessings Jacob pronounces over Joseph.

evidence.note: The wording pairs the disputed noun with enduring hills. The surrounding comparison concerns the reach or abundance of blessings.

words.summary: The phrase can also be read as what is desirable or choice about the hills. The boundary reading is uncertain.

senses.definition: Be startled by a sight that overturns an expectation.

evidence.note: The king rises hastily and asks how many men were thrown into the fire. He sees four walking free.

senses.definition: React with amazement to a person or be unsettled by a report.

evidence.note: The crowd sees Jesus, is amazed, and runs to greet him.

senses.definition: The dismay of nations faced with overwhelming sights and sounds.

evidence.note: The upheaval of the sea accompanies bewilderment on earth.

evidence.locator: Aramaic תְּוָא II, V00137, Targum to Ezekiel 9:4
evidence.note: The cognate occurs in a translation of the Hebrew marking scene.

cognates.note: Mandaic. The dictionary treats the order of the middle sounds as a transposition.

evidence.locator: s.v. tihua, scan leaf 259, citing Q 59:28 and CP 117, last line
Book I, p. 323, root توه, n4210
evidence.note: Perplexity is explicit, alongside the concrete sense of losing one’s way.

note: תָּוֶךְ and תִּיכוֹן belong to tavek. Most tokens of w.ai.ac are desire from אוה, so no count key is assigned for the disputed boundary in Gen 49:26. The independent noun or participle תּוֹלָל in Psa 137:3 has a repeated lamed and no demonstrated derivation from marking or astonishment. The name Toah/Tohu (Tohu@1Sa.1.1) contains ח, not the ה in this root; its origin is uncertain. No name assigned. SEDRA lexemes 3375 and 3376 attest the Syriac senses. No direct evidence establishes a link between Hebrew marking and Aramaic amazement.
